record.paper_title: A collection of open problems in celebration of Imre Leader’s 60th birthday
record.original_question: Find further applications of Pinto’s alternative-compression idea: situations where no single compression operator is guaranteed to preserve the desired monotonicity in every case, but where bad behavior cannot occur simultaneously across a larger collection of compressions, allowing a compression proof to go through.

evidence.quote: Question 10.2. Find some more applications where this twist on the compression method can be used to rescue a compression proof. That is, arguments in which any single compression operator is not guaranteed to behave well in all situations, but where this bad behaviour cannot occur simultaneously for a larger collection of compressions.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In extremal set theory, a compression operator is a map $C: \mathcal{P}([n]) \to \mathcal{P}([n])$ (extended to families of sets) that replaces each set with a "compressed" version (for example, the $ij$-compression sends a set $A$ to $(A\setminus\{j\})\cup\{i\}$ when $i\notin A$, $j\in A$ and this replacement is allowed, and to $A$ otherwise). Compression proofs typically establish an extremal inequality by showing that some monotone quantity (e.g. the size of the shadow, the number of edges, or a similar functional $\Phi$) does not increase under each compression in a fixed family $\mathcal{C}$, and then reducing to a "compressed" family that is easier to analyze.

The classical method requires that every single compression $C\in\mathcal{C}$ individually preserves the desired monotonicity in every situation. There is a strengthened variant — call it the alternative-compression method — in which one only requires the following weaker property: for every family $\mathcal{F}$, there exists at least one compression $C\in\mathcal{C}$ such that applying $C$ to $\mathcal{F}$ does not violate the monotonicity. Equivalently, the "bad" situations for different compressions in $\mathcal{C}$ never occur simultaneously, so at each step one can choose a compression that behaves well, even though no individual compression is guaranteed to behave well in every case.

Problem. Exhibit new applications of the alternative-compression method: identify and prove extremal combinatorial results (for instance in extremal set theory, intersecting-family problems, or shadow/Kruskal–Katona-type inequalities) where no single compression in a natural collection $\mathcal{C}$ is guaranteed to preserve the relevant monotone quantity, but where for every configuration at least one compression in $\mathcal{C}$ does, and use this to push through a compression proof that the standard single-compression approach cannot complete.
artifact.category_tag: Compression methods in extremal set theory
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is a research direction posed as an open question in a 2023 collection of open problems honoring Imre Leader. No follow-up work specifically applying Pinto's alternative-compression twist to new extremal problems was located.
